summary: Jesus calls Matthew from the toll-house, eats with tax collectors and sinners, and answers his critics with Hosea’s word on mercy.

context.title: The call of Matthew
paragraphs: Mark and Luke tell the same call but name the man Levi, and commentators generally take Levi and Matthew to be one person. [c1] The name Matthew is usually explained as “gift of God”. [c2] In its list of the Twelve, this Gospel calls him “Matthew the tax collector”, keeping his old trade in view. [c3]

Matthew sat at a toll-house, probably the customs post at Capernaum by the lake, where duty was levied on goods passing through. [c4] Tax-farming lent itself to extortion, and Jewish collectors working for Rome were widely despised. [c5] Rabbinic law reflects this reputation: a tax-gatherer could serve neither as a judge nor as a witness. [c6]

Luke says that the meal was a great feast that Levi gave in his own house. [c7] The objectors were Pharisees, whose members pledged themselves to Levitical purity and kept the purity of the Temple even at their daily meals, avoiding close contact with the careless. [c8] On table fellowship with publicans and sinners, Jesus differed sharply from them. [c9]

The Jewish Encyclopedia adds that on the main doctrine Jesus fully agreed with the Pharisees, so the dispute here is about practice within Israel. [c10] Jesus answers from Israel’s own prophet, quoting Hosea 6:6, and only Matthew includes the citation in this scene. [c11] He quotes the same line again in Mt 12:7, in a dispute about the Sabbath. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Telōnion names a fixed customs post, the place where tolls were assessed, not the tax itself.
translationNotes.body: Thayer gives two senses for telōnion, the toll itself and the toll-house where the collector sat, and files this verse under the second. [c13] Vincent explains that sitting at the office meant sitting on its raised bench, which stood for the whole establishment. [c14] Older English rendered the phrase “receipt of custom”, while the Revised Version has “place of toll”, which keeps the sense of a place. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: A fixed pairing in the Gospels: “sinners” here are people known for definite wrongdoing, not everyone.
translationNotes.body: Thayer distinguishes two uses of hamartōlos: anyone not free from sin, and people marked by definite vices, such as tax-gatherers. [c16] He files the pairing in this verse under the second use, but places the sinners of verse 13 under the first, where all are sinners. [c17] Ellicott adds that the word may have included Gentiles here, though it does not have to mean them. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: Literally “the strong”: Matthew and Mark use a word of strength, where Luke has the plainer medical “healthy”.
translationNotes.body: Ischyontes literally means those who are strong, and Luke’s parallel uses hygiainontes, those in health. [c19] Mark 2:17 has the same word as Matthew. [c20] Commentators hear a touch of irony in the proverb: the strong are those who think themselves whole, so Jesus answers his critics on their own terms. [c21]

original.gloss: mercy I want and not sacrifice

translationNotes.summary: Eleos stands for Hosea’s ḥesed, steadfast kindness; “and not” is a Hebrew way of saying “rather than”.
translationNotes.body: In Hosea 6:6 the Hebrew word is ḥesed, which BDB defines as goodness or kindness, though it suggests piety toward God in this verse. [c22] Thayer files the Greek eleos here under the readiness of people to help those in trouble. [c23] The form “mercy and not sacrifice” is a Hebrew way of stating a preference, not a rejection of sacrifice, which God had himself commanded. [c24]

claims.text: Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 name the tax collector called at the toll-house Levi, and the identification of Levi with Matthew is generally accepted.
The name Matthew is explained as meaning “gift of God”.
In the list of the Twelve in Mt 10:3, Matthew is called “the tax collector”, and this Gospel keeps his former occupation in view.
The toll-house was probably the custom-house of the lake at Capernaum, where customs were levied on produce passing in and out.
Roman customs dues were farmed out and lent themselves to extortion, making publicans unpopular, especially Jews exploiting their fellow Jews.
Tax-gatherers were ineligible to serve as judges or as witnesses (Sanh. 25b).
Luke 5:29 says that Levi made a great feast for Jesus in his own house.
Members of the Pharisaic brotherhood pledged strict observance of Levitical purity, observed at daily meals the purity of the priest in the Temple, and avoided close association with the ʿam ha-areẓ.
On intercourse with the ʿam ha-areẓ, the publican and the sinner, Jesus differed widely from the Pharisees.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Jesus fully agreed with the Pharisees on the main doctrine.
Jesus cites Hosea 6:6, and among the parallel accounts only Matthew gives the reference to Hosea.
Jesus cites Hosea 6:6 again in Mt 12:7, in reference to the Sabbath.
Thayer gives τελώνιον the senses customs or toll, and toll-house or place of toll, citing Mt 9:9 under the second.
Sitting at the toll-office means sitting on its elevated bench, which stood for the whole establishment.
The Authorised Version has “receipt of custom” and the Revised Version “place of toll”.
Thayer distinguishes ἁμαρτωλός in the sense not free from sin from the sense of men stained with definite vices, such as tax-gatherers.
Thayer lists the combination τελῶναι καὶ ἁμαρτωλοί in Mt 9:10 under the sense of definite vices, and Mt 9:13 under the sense in which all men are sinners.
Ellicott says that “sinners” may have included Gentiles but does not necessarily designate them.
Οἱ ἰσχύοντες literally means “they that are strong”, and Luke 5:31 has οἱ ὑγιαίνοντες, “they that are in health”.
Mark 2:17 uses the same word ἰσχύοντες as Mt 9:12.
There is irony in the saying: “the whole” are those who think themselves whole.
Hosea 6:6 uses חֶסֶד, which BDB glosses goodness, kindness, and for Hos 6:6 possibly piety toward God.
Thayer lists ἔλεος in Mt 9:13 under human readiness to help those in trouble.
“Mercy and not sacrifice” is a Hebrew mode of speaking meaning a preference for mercy, not a rejection of the sacrifices God had appointed.
